newsitem.title: INDIA: India expects huge growth in capital markets.
newsitem.headline: India expects huge growth in capital markets.

text.p: India will witness a sharp rise in the amount of funds raised by companies from the capital markets, D.R. Mehta, chairman of the regulatory Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) said on Tuesday.
"In the current year, 130 billion rupees ($3.6 billion) have been raised already," Mehta told a business conference on competition policy in the Indian capital.
"Hopefully, in the next few years, the Indian market can yield 1,000 billion rupees ($28 billion) annually," he added.
The current financial year, 1996/97, ends on March 31.

India axed many socialist controls on capital issues and share pricing under an economic reform programme launched in 1991, and allowed merchant bankers to assess share issues, until then subject to strict scrutiny by the finance ministry.
Private mutual funds and foreign institutional investors (FIIs) entered the market in a big way after the start of the reforms to end a monopoly by state-controlled mutual funds in India's bourses.
"SEBI believes in competition," Mehta said. "There has to be fierce competition."
Mehta said SEBI had approved as many as 400 merchant bankers who could scrutinise share issues, and did not limit their number because it wanted the market to arrive at a balance by itself.
Only 20 of the 400 merchant bankers accounted for 60 percent of the business, Mehta said. "A large number of merchant bankers today are not applying for renewal (of registration)," he said.
India has 22 stock exchanges, 9,000 brokers, 400 share registries, 34 domestic mutual funds, 434 FIIs and 12 custodians of mutual funds, making stock market regulation a challenging task, Mehta said.
There were 12 approved foreign brokers operating on Indian bourses, and more might be given permission, he said.
"We are not fond of over-regulation," Mehta said, but added that SEBI had to be alert to ensure that funds raised from small investors were properly used by firms that tapped their savings.
"The investor must be well briefed. That is why we have upgraded our disclosure norms," Mehta said. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
